common_name: Bearberry Cotoneaster (Evergreen Trailing Groundcover with Red Berries)

planting.note: Set container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained soil; space widely since stems root as they trail and knit into a dense mat within a few seasons.

directions: Bearberry cotoneaster hugs the ground on trailing stems clothed in small glossy evergreen leaves, making it a durable choice for covering slopes, cascading over walls, or filling gaps between stepping stones. Clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are followed by bright red berries that hang on through much of the winter, feeding birds when little else is available. It thrives in lean, well-drained soil and full sun, tolerating heat, wind, and salt spray once established, and needs only occasional shearing to keep it within bounds. Avoid heavy, poorly drained soils, which can encourage root and stem dieback.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil; mass plants on the spacing given for quicker fill as a low, dense groundcover.

directions: This selection of bearberry cotoneaster forms a low, tight mound of arching stems rather than the flatter mat of the species, giving it a fuller, more finished look in foundation plantings and parking lot islands. Small white flowers in spring give way to an especially heavy set of coral-orange berries that persist well into winter and stand out against the small dark evergreen leaves. It tolerates poor soil, drought, and urban conditions once established, and benefits from an occasional hard cutback every few years to renew dense growth and prevent the center from thinning out. Good drainage is essential, as waterlogged roots invite dieback.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil; allow ample room for its ultimate size or use as an informal hedge on tighter spacing with annual shearing.

directions: Willowleaf cotoneaster is a large, fountain-shaped evergreen shrub with long narrow leaves resembling willow foliage on gracefully arching branches, giving it a softer texture than most cotoneasters. Flat clusters of small white flowers cover the plant in late spring, followed by heavy clusters of red berries that weight the branch tips through fall and into winter. It adapts to a wide range of soils as long as drainage is adequate, tolerates heat and some drought, and can be left informal as a large screen or pruned up into a small multi-stem tree. Give it plenty of room, since crowding leads to a congested, hard-to-maintain thicket.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil; this is one of the hardiest cotoneasters and suits exposed sites in colder climates where C. horizontalis may struggle.

directions: Cranberry cotoneaster shares the stiff herringbone branching of its relative C. horizontalis but grows a bit taller and bears rounder, glossier leaves and noticeably larger, cranberry-red fruit. Pinkish-white flowers open along the branches in late spring, followed by the showy fall berry display that gives the plant its common name and its excellent winter interest. Foliage often takes on bronze-red tones in autumn before dropping, and the plant tolerates rocky, dry, or exposed sites with minimal care beyond occasional shaping. It is among the most cold-hardy cotoneasters, making it a dependable choice where winter exposure limits other broadleaf shrubs.

common_name: Milkflower Cotoneaster (Evergreen Hedging Shrub with Winter Berries)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil; space on the tighter end for a solid hedge or wider for a specimen screening shrub.

directions: Milkflower cotoneaster is a dense, upright evergreen shrub with leathery, deeply veined dark green leaves that have a felted gray-white underside, giving the foliage a two-toned look in the wind. Clusters of small milky-white flowers open in early summer and are followed by long-lasting orange-red berries that ripen in autumn and often hold well into late winter, making it a favorite for winter birds. It takes well to shearing and is widely used as a screening hedge or windbreak, tolerating heat, wind, and a range of soils as long as drainage is reasonable. Renewal-prune older plants occasionally to keep the base from becoming bare and leggy.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil; works well as an informal unclipped hedge or pruned into a loose screen.

directions: Franchet's cotoneaster is an arching, fountain-shaped shrub with gray-green leaves that are downy underneath, giving the foliage a soft, silvery cast that sets it apart from the glossier dark-leaved species. Small pink-tinged white flowers appear in late spring, followed by an abundant crop of orange-red berries that persist through much of the winter and are readily taken by birds. It handles heat, wind, and poor soil well once established and is commonly grown as an informal hedge or background screen where its graceful, slightly weeping branches can be left unclipped. In mild winters it holds much of its foliage, while colder winters cause it to drop leaves and behave more like a deciduous shrub.

common_name: Spreading Cotoneaster (Deciduous Shrub with Red Fall Foliage)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil; suits informal hedging or mixed shrub borders where its fall color and berry display can be appreciated up close.

directions: Spreading cotoneaster forms a dense, gracefully arching mound of fine-textured branches lined with small dark green leaves that turn shades of red and purple in fall, among the best autumn color in the genus. Small pinkish flowers in late spring lead to dark red berries that ripen alongside the changing foliage, giving a two-season display of color on the same branches. It is adaptable to a range of well-drained soils, tolerates urban conditions and light shearing, and rarely needs more than occasional thinning to remove old wood. Its dense branching also makes it a useful informal barrier hedge that requires little upkeep beyond an annual shaping.
